extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, judges, and law students
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and doctrinal criteria governing the validity, effect, construction, recording, and remedies for assignments and related transfers (licenses, powers of attorney, contracts to assign) of inventions, patents, extensions, and inchoate patent rights in U.S. practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignments governed wholly by statute
rubrics_metrics.description: That assignments are governed wholly by statute; an assignment is not valid unless it complies with the laws of the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citations given (e.g., Suydam v. Day). Emphasizes statutory compliance as a threshold requirement for validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment must be in writing and signed by the assignors
rubrics_metrics.description: That an assignment must be in writing, and be signed by the assignors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple cases cited (e.g., Gottfried v. Miller). This is repeatedly stated as a formal requirement for a valid assignment (distinguishing assignments from mere parol agreements).

rubrics_metrics.name: Instrument must contain operative words unequivocally indicating intention to convey interest in invention and monopoly
rubrics_metrics.description: It must also contain operative words unequivocally indicating an intention to convey an interest both in the invention and in the monopoly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No particular form required, but there must be some operative language expressing an intention to assign (see Campbell v. James, Wheeler, J.). The construction of the instrument determines whether it is an assignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: No special form required for assignment
rubrics_metrics.description: That an assignment requires no special form; no particular form is required; but there must be operative words expressing at least an intention to assign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although form is not prescribed, courts construe the instrument's language to ascertain intent; absence of specific formalities does not render an assignment void if intent is clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parol evidence cannot vary assignment terms except for mutual mistake
rubrics_metrics.description: Parol evidence is not admissible to vary the terms of an assignment except in cases of mutual mistake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will construe the written instrument; extrinsic evidence generally excluded except to show mutual mistake (see Knowlton Platform & Car Coupling Co. v. Cook).

rubrics_metrics.name: Parol agreements can create equitable title enforceable in equity
rubrics_metrics.description: A parol agreement to assign may pass an equitable title which a court of equity will enforce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parol contracts may create equitable interests and may be specifically enforced when appropriate (e.g., Burr v. De La Vergne; Whitney v. Burr). Such equitable interests, however, have limits when facing subsequent legal-title holders without notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignments may be made before or after patent issue (assignability of inchoate rights)
rubrics_metrics.description: An assignment of a completed invention may be made either before or after the issue of the patent. An inventor has an inchoate right to the monopoly prior to patent grant, and that inchoate right is assignable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An assignment covering inchoate rights and properly recorded secures the assignee both the invention and monopoly immediately on issuance; assignment before patent is favored in law but has procedural requirements to obtain legal title on issuance.

rubrics_metrics.name: To have patent issued directly to assignee, instrument must request issue to assignee and be recorded before final fee
rubrics_metrics.description: To authorize issue of the patent directly to the assignee, the instrument of assignment must contain a written request to the Commissioner of Patents that the letters-patent may be granted to the assignee (or assignee and inventor if undivided interest), and must be filed for record in the Patent Office before the date fixed for payment of the final fee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If these steps are complied with, the legal title vests in the assignee on issuance. Cases cited (e.g., Gayler v. Wilder; Wright v. Randell) illustrate strict timing and content requirements for recording to effect issuance to assignee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to request issue or timely record conveys only equitable title (not legal title)
rubrics_metrics.description: An instrument purporting to be an assignment but not containing the written request or not recorded in due season does not convey the legal title to the patented invention; it may create an equitable title enforceable in chancery but cannot prevail over a later bona fide assignee who obtains legal title without notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes difference between legal and equitable title; equitable assignee may be treated as beneficiary/owner in equity but is vulnerable to intervening legal transfers recorded according to statute (see Wright v. Randell; Davis Wagon Wheel Co. v. Davis Wagon Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent cannot issue to assignee unless assignment requests that effect and is duly entered for record
rubrics_metrics.description: That the patent cannot issue to the assignee unless the assignment contains a request to that effect and is duly entered for record as prescribed by the rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrative/recording formalities in the Patent Office are necessary to transfer issuance rights; failure may mean the patent issues to the inventor even though an assignment exists in equity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recording priority and effect of successive assignments on record
rubrics_metrics.description: Where several successive assignees' assignments were on record pending the application, the title vests in the last of those on record (i.e., priority among recorded assignments is governed by record dates and statutory rules).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited case: Consolidated Electric Light Co. v. McKeesport Light Co. Explains interaction of multiple assignments filed during pendency and which recorded assignment controls issuance and title.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent Office cannot take notice of contingent equitable interests
rubrics_metrics.description: The Patent Office cannot take notice of an equitable interest whose existence is contingent on the issuing of a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equitable interests contingent on issuance are not recognized administratively; they must rely on later court enforcement. (See Martin v. Olney.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment of future inventions is an executory contract, not an assignment
rubrics_metrics.description: A contract for the transfer of inventions not yet in being is valid as a contract, but is not an assignment; the subject-matter of an assignment is an existing invention actually reduced to practice (inchoate or perfected right), while intended or incomplete inventions remain mere executory contracts to assign if later completed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such contracts bind parties and may be specifically enforced in equity when completed and when third-party interests absent, but they do not create present assignable patent title (see §771 and cases like Ex parte Edison).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment of extensions: effect and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: When law provides for grant of an extension to a patentee, he may assign his right to the extension in the same manner, even before the original patent has been issued. Such an assignment creates an equitable title which becomes operative on grant of the extension, vesting invention and monopoly per the conveyance terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assignments of extension rights may be made before grant; equitable title becomes legal on grant. Assignments of extensions may be specifically enforced; an agreement to assign an extension is valid in equity (cases: Consolidated Fruit Jar Co. v. Mason; Ex parte Holmes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Extent of assignee's interest determined by assignor's interest and conveyance terms
rubrics_metrics.description: The extent of the interest created in the assignee by an assignment depends in part upon the interest owned by the assignor and in part upon the terms of the conveyance; an assignor cannot transfer what he does not possess.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even broad language in a conveyance operates only within the scope of rights vested in the assignor at assignment date. Multiple instruments forming a transaction are construed together; parol evidence only for mutual mistake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignee takes subject to prior lawful conveyances, licenses and restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: The assignee must take his interest subject to all previous lawful conveyances and to the restrictions originally imposed upon his assignor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the assignor's interest was already limited (previous grants, irrevocable licenses), the assignee receives only the residuary or reversionary rights that remain; courts will not presume grant of rights the assignor lacked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irrevocable power of attorney can, depending on form, operate as assignment
rubrics_metrics.description: An irrevocable power of attorney, giving full control over the patented invention (e.g., 'sole agent' for making and selling with proceeds remitted), may vest entire ownership in the attorney named and, although differing in form from conveyance, may be a true assignment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether a power of attorney constitutes an assignment depends on its terms and effect; courts look to substance over form (see Hartshorn v. Day; Hartsborn v. Day citations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment executed by attorney in his own name is invalid; owner's signature essential
rubrics_metrics.description: That an assignment executed by an attorney in his own name is invalid; the signature of the owner being essential in certain contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attorney must execute in manner that shows principal's consent/authorization; improper formality may render assignment ineffective (see Pryor v. Coulter).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sale before patent issues secures rights to vendee upon issuance
rubrics_metrics.description: A sale by the inventor before the patent issues secures the invention to the vendee after the patent is granted (i.e., vendee's rights follow upon issuance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such pre-issue sales can operate to transfer the right contingent on issuance; if properly documented, the vendee obtains the benefit when patent issues (see Rathbone v. Orr).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment of 'all the rights' warrants perfect title
rubrics_metrics.description: An assignment of 'all the rights' to the patented invention, in whatever language such rights may be described, transfers or attempts to transfer the entire interest covered by the patent and warrants a perfect title (i.e., imports an assertion of sole ownership).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the assignor truly has unqualified ownership, assignee gets exclusive title; if not, the assignee may have remedy for breach of implied warranty or may treat transfer as void.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment of 'all my rights' implies no warranty of title
rubrics_metrics.description: An assignment of 'all the rights of the assignor' in the patented invention contains no implied averment as to the nature or scope of the interest conveyed and therefore implies no warranty that the assignor owned the entire right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such conveyance transfers whatever interest the assignor then had, subject to prior conveyances; assignee cannot claim implied perfect title where instrument limited to assignor's existing rights (see Tumbull v. Weir Plow Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment imports implied warranty that assignor has good right to convey and remedies for breach
rubrics_metrics.description: The assignment imports a covenant that the assignor has a good right to convey the interest described; when assigned interest exceeds what he could convey, the assignee has a remedy for breach of warranty (action on implied warranty) or may treat transfer void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts examine the wording to determine warranty scope; remedies include damages or rescission depending on circumstances (see discussion in §774-775).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conveyances construed to effect parties' intention; practical construction may control
rubrics_metrics.description: Conveyances are to be construed so as to effect the intention of the parties; where in doubt the practical construction given to the contract by the acts of the parties may control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts interpret grants to cover whatever is necessary to render them effective; multiple instruments forming a transaction are read together (see Nicholson Pave­ment Co. v. Jenkins; Topliff v. Topliff).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific performance and equitable relief limited by equities of parties
rubrics_metrics.description: A contract to assign (including before patent) may be specifically enforced in equity, but a court will not decree specific performance where the petitioner has not acted equitably or where performance has been rendered impossible through fraudulent acts of the defendant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equitable remedies are discretionary — courts will refuse relief when petitioner repeatedly breached contract or when enforcing would avail nothing (cases: Hapgood v. Rosenstock; Kennedy v. Hazelton; Werden v. Graham).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignments of part rights and of improvements: scope and acceptance rules
rubrics_metrics.description: An assignment of part (e.g., 'one third of the full and exclusive right') in a specification about to be filed carries the stated fractional interest in all patentable devices described and claimed; an assignee may accept a different patent in lieu of the one agreed to if he acts on such acceptance and is estopped from claiming the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assignments purporting to cover future improvements/devices included in a specification can vest proportional interest; courts have enforced acceptance and estoppel doctrines (see Puetz v. Bransford; Topliff v. Topliff).
